chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fazzal, from Thal'abah ibn Maymoun, from Umar ibn Abi Bakkar, from Abu Bakr Al-Hadrami, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) married Miqdad ibn Al-Aswad to Zuba'ah, daughter of Al-Zubayr ibn Abd al-Muttalib. And he married him for the marriages to be humble/modest, and for them to follow the example of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), and for them to know that the most noble of them in the sight of Allah is the most pious of them.

key_terms.الزُّبَيْرِ بْنِ عَبْدِ الْمَُطَّلِبِ: Al-Zubayr ibn Abd al-Muttalib, uncle of the Prophet
key_terms.لِتَتَّضِعَ الْمَنَاكِحُ: For marriages to be humble/modest (not ostentatious)
key_terms.مِقْدَادَ بْنَ الْأَسْوَدِ: Miqdad ibn Al-Aswad, a prominent companion

ai.seo_question: Why did the Prophet (SAWW) marry Miqdad to Zuba'ah and what does it teach about nobility in Islam?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Kafi records the Prophet Muhammad's (SAW) marriage of Miqdad ibn Al-Aswad to Zuba'ah bint Al-Zubayr, a union that served as a practical lesson in humility (tadhi' al-manakih) for the community. Shia scholars emphasize this event to illustrate that the Prophet's marital choices were deliberate pedagogical acts, reinforcing the Quranic principle that true nobility lies in taqwa (piety) rather than lineage or wealth.
